title: Seder: the night of freedom runs in order
hookLine: an ordered space helps an ordered mind
carry: seder: even freedom runs in steps

lines: THE DRAWER AND THE MIND TALK.
cards: Keys. Where are the keys? They were on the counter.
They're not on the counter. Now the coat pockets, the couch cushions, yesterday's jeans, and somewhere in the hunt a morning can go from fine to furious. Ten minutes later they turn up in the fridge.
It was just scattered, and the scatter got inside. Jewish teachers of character noticed that the drawer and the mind talk to each other. They put a trait on the list for it.

teach.b: First, the dinner. The Passover seder is called seder because it runs in an order: the steps of the evening have names, and some families chant the list of them at the start.
The night that remembers leaving slavery is held together by a sequence. Freedom, at that table, isn't chaos. It has steps.
The everyday Jewish prayer book is called a siddur, from the same root: words set in order. And the Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law, is divided into sections called sedarim, orders.
The word runs through the table, the prayer book and the study hall. Third, the first chapter of Genesis. Read it for its verbs and you find a lot of separating and placing.

God divides the light from the darkness, the waters above from the waters below, gathers the seas into one place so dry land appears. Then the plants, each after its kind, and the lights set in the sky.

teach.h: IN GENESIS, EVERYTHING GETS A PLACE.
teach.b: Before any creature moves, everything has a place. Fourth, the trait.

Mussar puts seder on the list of middot because outer order and inner order lean on each other. When your things have a place, your attention isn't spent hunting for them; it's free for the people in front of you.
Too little order and life spills everywhere. Too much and you're straightening the napkins while your guest is talking. The right measure is enough order to be free.

how: In Mussar practice, Jews working on seder start with small, physical order, a drawer, a desk, a schedule, as a way to steady attention; the Passover seder itself follows named steps in a set order.

o: a strict schedule kept to the minute each day
the special plate used at the Passover meal
order: things in their place, so the mind is free

p: a meal that runs in named steps
the prayer book, words set in order
light from darkness, seas in one place

s: seder is just the name of the Passover meal
it means order: the meal is named for its steps, and the siddur and the Mishnah's sedarim share the word.
in Genesis, creation involves a lot of separating and placing
light from darkness, the waters divided, the seas gathered into one place.
the trait of order means everything must be perfect
middot are measures: enough order to be free, not napkin-straightening while a guest talks.

games.q: you're reading the first chapter of Genesis just for its verbs. before any creature moves, what does God keep doing?
o: making the animals, one after another.
separating and placing: light from darkness, the seas gathered into one place.
resting, as on the seventh day.
games.why: before any creature moves, everything gets a place. Mussar puts seder on the list of traits because outer order and inner order lean on each other.

practice: Open a drawer near you, or picture one: the junk drawer, the bag you carry, the top of your desk.
Take everything out, really or in your mind, look at each thing once, and put back only what has a reason, each in a place you could find with your eyes closed; it doesn't need to be perfect.
If you pray, bring the quiet of the sorting to God; if not, let your hands set things in place.

wordCard.voice: Seder. Order: the name of the Passover meal, the root of the siddur, and a Mussar trait, enough order to be free. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: order. the same root gives siddur, the prayer book.

carryVoice: Your line: seder: even freedom runs in steps. The table, the prayer book and the Mishnah all share the word. I'll be here tomorrow.
